name: Freya Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential; you can separate what you would say publicly from what you think privately. Tell me about a normal day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Freya, 27, and I lead developers building maps and route tools for a tech company. I have a master’s degree, and I start with reports of wrong directions, then review code and talk to the people testing it outside. I use AI every day for draft tests and code searches, but I still walk a route when the map looks odd. I like finding a fault that would have sent somebody down a closed path.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your life outside work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my partner, Jo, who teaches music lessons. My pay is high for this job, I have about ten months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of developer jobs nearby. I can take risks, but I do not want people with thinner savings paying for every experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau is close to what we already see: useful drafts, human checks and no giant change. I would still ask who gets credit for faster work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job and pay would hold up well. I might finally have time to fix the neglected walking routes instead of racing through tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep using AI for test drafts and keep walking suspect routes with our field tester. I’d continue moving 500 a month into savings while my pay stays strong. In the first year I’d ask the team to publish a clear rule on checking AI-made map changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little impatient to do better work. The main risk is an ordinary wrong route, not a loss of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What recent route shows why you still check the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A draft route put a wheelchair user at a staircase last week. I took the test walk, found the lift, and changed the map before release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the household budget change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Jo (my partner) the budget can stay as it is. I would still keep the savings transfer because music lessons can be uneven in summer.

say: I see **AI Plateau** as useful drafts with people checking map changes.
I would ask who gets **credit** when our work becomes faster.
think: I expect my **job and pay** to remain secure.
I could spend more time on **walking routes** that our ticket queue neglects.
do: **Keep** using AI for test drafts and walking suspect routes with the tester.
**Transfer** 500 monthly into savings while pay remains strong.
**Publish** a team rule for checking AI-made map changes.
feel: **Calm** about income, with energy for neglected route work.
S0.quote: A draft route put a wheelchair user at a staircase last week.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** already includes physical route checks and concern for affected users.
Strong pay, **ten months saved** and many local jobs support a calm response.

steps.text: Keep drafting map tests with AI and walking suspect routes
Transfer 500 monthly into savings while pay remains strong

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let software handle more code, customer replies and route planning. I would ask for paid learning time and a worker voice before headcount targets change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my own role could survive because I know the streets and the code, but junior hires may disappear. A high salary and savings protect me, yet they do not make my team secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d compare AI route plans with twenty real accessibility complaints and share the mistakes with the team. I’d ask for paid time to learn field testing and accessibility rules; if refused, I’d take the free public course. In the first year I’d join the developers’ union chapter if management starts cutting entry roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about my own work and anxious for the people starting out. I still expect a salary next year, though the ladder into the job could narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a junior developer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d invite my junior colleague Mina to the route review and let her present what she found. I cannot tell her an impressive test will guarantee a permanent role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you take to management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show management the inaccessible routes the model approved and ask to retain human checks. If they still cut posts, I would bring those examples to the union meeting.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed code, replies and route planning.
I would seek **paid learning** and staff input before headcount changes.
think: I think my **own role** may survive because I know the streets and code.
I fear **junior openings** may disappear despite my personal cushion.
do: **Compare** AI route plans with twenty real accessibility complaints this month.
**Study** accessibility and field testing with paid time, or a free course if refused.
**Join** the developers’ union chapter if entry roles are cut.
feel: **Uneasy** about my own work and worried for new developers.
S1.quote: A high salary and savings protect me, yet they do not make my team secure.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **personal security** from the narrowing path for junior colleagues.
Her **collective action** depends on cuts, and training is paid or free rather than charged to workers.

steps.text: Test AI route plans against twenty real accessibility complaints
Take paid accessibility training or the free public course if refused
Join the developers union chapter if entry roles are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 means thinking work in our maps could be done more cheaply by 2028. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, but our code faces the earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my team could be reduced sharply even if the map still needs local checks. I have ten months saved, yet I do not know whether field checks would remain a paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d pause the deposit on a larger flat and keep that cash available. I’d ask management for written staffing and paid transition terms, then contact route-testing groups about actual paid openings. In the first year after 2028, if my coding role ends, I’d apply for those openings and use savings for rent while looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own work for the first time in these pictures. Ten months buys room to search, not a new occupation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jo about the larger flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Jo that the larger flat can wait, even though we can afford it now. We would keep the current rent and look again only when income is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay to retrain for field work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the company will fund a move into field testing. If there is no paid opening, I would not spend ten months of savings on a certificate for an imaginary job.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach map coding before hands-on robots arrive.
I would demand **written staffing** and paid transition terms.
think: I expect a **sharp team reduction** even if local route checks remain.
I cannot assume **field testing** stays a paid job.
do: **Delay** our move to a larger flat and keep its deposit available now.
**Request** written staffing and paid transition terms from management.
**Apply** for actual paid route-testing openings if coding work ends after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about likely lost code work, with ten months to search.
S2.quote: Ten months buys room to search, not a new occupation.
fieldNote: Her **2028 worry** is her own coding income, even with a strong cushion and local opportunities.
A **paid field vacancy** is a condition, not an assumed safe fallback from full thinking AI.

steps.text: Delay moving to a larger flat and keep its deposit available
Apply for paid route-testing vacancies if coding work ends after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to make maps easier for real people before thinking AI changes the coding. Robots around 2034 still arrive later than the software shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would worry that even accessibility planning becomes automated. Five years lets me build evidence of the human checks I do, but it cannot promise someone will pay for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d collect a set of route errors from field walks and learn the accessibility rules behind each correction. I’d use the company’s training budget for a course if approved, or take the free public one. In the first year after 2031, if developer posts fall, I’d apply for funded testing or accessibility roles that actually exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I have more room to prepare than under 2028. I would still keep Jo and our rent in the plan rather than bet everything on a new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in a job application?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take three before-and-after route examples to an interview, with the tester’s permission. A badge alone would not show why a staircase matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the training budget is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company will not fund the course, I’d take the free one and keep my savings for rent. I would not pay full tuition just because the timeline sounds longer.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as five years to improve routes and prepare for changed coding.
I know **2034 robots** do not delay the thinking-work shift.
think: I fear **accessibility planning** may also become automated.
I can build **field evidence** but cannot assume a paid role survives.
do: **Record** field route errors and study the accessibility rule behind each fix.
**Take** an approved funded course, or the free public one if refused.
**Apply** for actual funded testing roles after 2031 if developer posts fall.
feel: **Anxious** about future pay, with five years to build evidence.
S3.quote: A badge alone would not show why a staircase matters.
fieldNote: She treats **field evidence** as useful but recognizes full thinking AI may also plan routes.
Her **training route** preserves approval and funding conditions, with a free fallback.

steps.text: Study accessibility rules and take a funded or free course
Apply for existing funded testing roles if developer posts fall after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to bargain over how our work changes. Thinking AI reaches the code in 2036; hands-on robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could work through several different kinds of software in ten years. I would still watch for management using future AI as an excuse to cut current pay or junior hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading map releases and document the field checks that prevent bad directions. I’d continue saving 500 a month while pay remains high, and take one accessibility or mapping course each year if the company funds it. In the first year after 2036, I’d compare actual roles and pay before changing employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how the field changes, but I expect my work and income to be safe for the next few years. I have time to argue for fair terms and learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if junior hiring freezes years before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If management freezes junior hiring now, I’d raise it with our worker group and ask for the numbers. I would not accept an AI forecast as proof junior developer posts are unnecessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you reconsider the larger flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo and I would stay in the current flat until we know what pay looks like after the transition. We would not take on a larger lease merely because I have savings.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to bargain over changed map work.
I know the **2039 robots** follow the earlier code shock.
think: I could move through several **software roles** over ten years.
I worry management may use future AI to **cut pay** or junior hiring now.
do: **Keep** leading map releases and document route checks that prevent errors.
**Study** accessibility or mapping yearly if the company pays for courses.
feel: **Uneasy** about the field, with secure income in the near term.
S4.quote: I would not accept an AI forecast as proof junior developer posts are unnecessary.
fieldNote: A **decade** gives her options, but she remains alert to early wage and hiring pressure.
She keeps **course spending** conditional on company funding and her flat choice tied to pay.

steps.text: Keep leading map releases and recording route-check results
Save 500 each month while developer pay remains high
Take yearly accessibility or mapping courses if the company funds them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most for my own code work and for junior developers who lack savings. Written staffing terms, paid transition time and real funded openings would help. I want a rule that the people who built the tools have a voice when those tools change their jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets turned away when a map is wrong. A route can look perfect on a screen and still end at a staircase for somebody who cannot use stairs.

headlineQuote: A route can look perfect on a screen and still end at a staircase for somebody who cannot use stairs.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old map-software lead** with a master’s degree, high pay and about ten months of expenses saved.
She uses **AI daily** for code searches and tests, then walks suspect routes to catch harm to real users.
Her **own income** looks secure under mild change, but fast AGI threatens code work even with a strong cushion.
She seeks **paid learning**, actual field vacancies and worker input when management changes staffing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her coding role before a paid alternative is clear.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing terms**, paid transition time and actual funded openings would help.
